articles.title: INTERVIEW: “Freight Forwarding is Evolving into End-to-End Supply Chain Orchestration”- Manisha Malhotra, DP World - India Shipping News
articles.summary: INTERVIEW: “Freight Forwarding is Evolving into End-to-End Supply Chain Orchestration”- Manisha Malhotra, DP World  India Shipping News
articles.full_text:
As global trade patterns shift and supply chains face growing demands for greater visibility, flexibility and resilience, freight forwarding is taking on a far more strategic role than simply moving cargo from one destination to another. For integrated logistics providers, the challenge lies in connecting infrastructure, multimodal transportation, warehousing and digital capabilities to deliver seamless end-to-end solutions. In an exclusive interaction with India Shipping News, Ms. Manisha Malhotra, Vice President – Freight Forwarding, SCO , DP World, shares her perspective on the changing dynamics of freight forwarding, the importance of integrated logistics networks, and the role of technology in building more agile and resilient supply chains. She also discusses opportunities for Indian exporters and importers to expand into global markets, particularly through stronger trade corridors linking India with the Middle East and Africa, and explains how integrated logistics can help strengthen India’s competitiveness in global trade.
Q: For many years, freight forwarding was largely perceived as a transactional service focused on moving cargo from one point to another. Today, however, it has evolved into a strategic component of supply chain management. How do you see the role of freight forwarding changing in the era of integrated logistics, and what should businesses expect from a modern freight forwarding partner?
- A: Today, customers increasingly expect real-time shipment visibility, predictive insights, digital documentation and proactive exception management that enable faster, better-informed decisions. In this scenario, flexible freight forwarding services will need to be built around customers’ cargo needs and technology enabled.
DP World views freight forwarding as a critical link within our integrated logistics ecosystem. By combining our global network of ports, terminals, inland logistics, rail, warehousing and freight forwarding, we enable cargo infrastructure and information to move together through one connected platform. This reduces coordination with multiple stakeholders, shortens transit times and improves supply chain efficiency.
From here on, businesses should expect a freight forwarding partner to act as a strategic advisor beyond just moving cargo efficiently. This will help them optimize supply chains, respond quickly to disruptions, access new markets and build long-term resilience in an increasingly dynamic global trade environment.
Q: DP World has steadily transformed itself from a global port operator into an end-to-end logistics solutions provider. How does freight forwarding complement your broader logistics ecosystem comprising port terminals, inland container depots, rail connectivity, warehousing and multimodal transport to create a seamless customer experience?
- A: DP World’s integrated approach enables smoother transitions across transport modes, reduces dwell times and improves overall supply chain efficiency.
Freight forwarding helps connect customers directly to our physical infrastructure, while our digital platforms, real-time cargo visibility and integrated warehouse technologies help them manage inventory more effectively and make faster, better-informed operational decisions, across the entire logistics journey.
In India, we operate through 11 freight forwarding offices, delivering end-to-end solutions for both containerised and project cargo across ocean and air freight. Combined with strong shipping line connectivity, global container availability, extensive trade lane coverage and specialised air freight network, we help customers navigate global trade with greater confidence, reliability and flexibility. With our global network of 300 + Freight Forwarding offices we are highly equipped to support businesses to reach new markets and achieve scale.
Q: Supply chains today are expected to deliver not only speed but also predictability, visibility and resilience. From your experience, what are the biggest operational challenges customers face today, and how does DP World’s integrated logistics network help them overcome these challenges?
A: In an increasingly dynamic trade environment, businesses diversify sourcing and expand into new markets, they are looking for integrated logistics partners that can simplify complexity and provide greater flexibility. Gartner research reinforces this shift, finding that only 29% of supply chain organisations[1] have developed the capabilities needed for future readiness, including agility, resilience and integrated ecosystems.
DP World enables customers to build resilient supply chains by connecting every stage through our own assets. Our port terminals, rail services, warehousing, multimodal transport, economic zones and contract logistics provide seamless end‑to‑end cargo movement and informed operational decision‑making. In India, this integrated network is strengthened by Free Trade Warehousing Zones in Nhava Sheva, Chennai and Cochin, supported by dedicated rail and multimodal infrastructure that enhance connectivity, flexibility and resilience.
This is complemented by our global network across more than 80 countries and partner operations, giving customers greater visibility and control over cargo. The advantage of owning assets is not only improved transparency but also the ability to navigate complex challenges. In times of disruption, it allows us to support businesses with flexible choices and dependable visibility throughout the supply chain.
Q: India is witnessing unprecedented investments in logistics infrastructure through initiatives such as PM Gati Shakti, Dedicated Freight Corridors and the National Logistics Policy. How is DP World aligning its freight forwarding strategy with these national initiatives, and what opportunities do you foresee for Indian exporters and importers?
- A: As per DP World’s Global Trade Observatory Annual Outlook Report 2026, more than half of businesses now prioritise supply chain diversification, while reaching new markets is their top growth objective. They are also evaluating new trade routes based on cost, connectivity and faster cargo clearance.
DP World is aligning its freight forwarding strategy by embedding Indian exporters into global corridors through initiatives such as Bharat Mart in JAFZA, this transformative marketplace will Indian businesses to 1.2 billion consumers across the Middle East.
At the same time, our own multimodal assets across India and Africa position us to strengthen the India–Africa trade corridor. With India–Africa trade already valued at nearly USD 94 billion, DP World’s integrated terminals, free trade zones and logistics parks provide exporters and importers with seamless access to high‑growth African markets. DP World freight forwarding network provides credibility to customers those who are looking at expanding in their operations in Africa region. Considering it’s a new market, the freight forwarding solutions can help navigate customers through regulatory challenges and provide optimum visibility of their cargo.
By leveraging our infrastructure in both regions, we are enabling Indian businesses particularly MSMEs to diversify supply chains, manage cargo flows efficiently, and capture new opportunities in global trade. This alignment ensures that as India advances its logistics ambitions, DP World continues to support exporters and importers with reliable, scalable and future‑ready freight forwarding solutions.
Q: Digitalisation is rapidly reshaping global logistics. From real-time shipment visibility and predictive analytics to digital documentation and customer platforms, technology is becoming a key differentiator. Which digital capabilities do you believe will define the next generation of freight forwarding services?
- A: India has made significant progress in digitizing logistics through initiatives such as ULIP, ICEGATE digital customs processes and paperless documentation. The next phase is focused on creating intelligent, connected supply chains where data moves as seamlessly as cargo.
Globally, technology is enabling shippers to anticipate disruption, optimise cargo flows and complete documentation digitally. At DP World, we are advancing this transformation through our Virtual Trade Corridor, which connects customs authorities, ports and customers on a single digital platform. This innovation reduces clearance times dramatically and allows cargo to move seamlessly across borders. Additionally, we have our own patented technology to deliver predictive analytics and integrated documentation across our global network.
Q: As global supply chains continue to diversify and businesses adopt the ‘China Plus One’ sourcing strategy, India has a unique opportunity to emerge as a preferred global manufacturing and export hub. In your view, what role will integrate logistics providers such as DP World play in strengthening India’s global competitiveness over the next decade?
- A: Global supply chains are diversifying, and India is emerging as a preferred hub. UNCTAD’s 2026 report highlights India gaining investment in electronics and electric vehicles, while Production Linked Incentive schemes have already catalysed trillions in exports and billions in manufacturing investment. Yet this success depends on reliable logistics, ensuring output reaches ships as seamlessly as it leaves factories.
DP World’s integrated ecosystem is designed for precisely this role. With terminals at Mundra and Nhava Sheva, a rail network linking key industrial centres, and the upcoming Tuna Tekra terminal adding 2.19 million TEUs of capacity, we provide the last mile between India’s manufacturing renaissance and global markets.

articles.title: US and Israel are warned against launching fresh strikes on Iran - The Guardian
articles.summary: US and Israel are warned against launching fresh strikes on Iran  The GuardianIstanbul meeting: A new division of labor in the Iran war?  Iran InternationalEuropean, Middle East ministers urge US-Iran diplomacy, not new attacks  Al JazeeraTurkey says renewed attack on Iran would expand conflict, diplomacy only way  ReutersEgypt, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Pakistan say 'Israeli occupation main source of regional instability'  The Times of Israel
articles.full_text:
Foreign ministers at a summit of eight European and Middle Eastern countries have urged the US and Israel not to renews their attacks on Iran, warning a fresh outbreak of fighting would spread conflict and push oil prices even higher.
The development of a new multinational “anti-war bloc” represents a challenge to the increasingly open plans by the US and Israel to relaunch strikes on Iran while talks on Tehran’s nuclear programme remain deadlocked.
The Turkish foreign minister, Hakan Fidan, joint convener of the summit in Istanbul, said: “Military intervention in Iran is not any kind of solution. We agreed that a new military attack would spread the war and the conflict in the region. All the countries around the table do not want the war to spread even more, once again.”
Ministers also demanded an end to the Houthi assaults on Saudi Arabia, and an immediate opening of the strait of Hormuz currently blockaded by Iranian ships and drones.
Jean-Noël Barrot, the French foreign minister, said another war between Iran and the US would be bad for both sides, and only worsen rising oil prices, which have hit their highest level since May. Ed Miliband, the UK foreign secretary, also urged both sides to embrace diplomacy.
The Istanbul meeting, an unprecedented gathering of regional and European leaders initiated by Turkey and Germany, represented a rare chance for European ministers to have any input into the crises afflicting the Middle East, including in Yemen, Palestine and Iran. They have largely been left as bystanders, apart from sending air force protection to Saudi Arabia as it tries to fend off Houthi drone and missile assaults on its airports and energy installations.
The Middle Eastern states were represented by Fidan, Egypt’s Badr Abdelatty, Pakistan’s Ishaq Dar and Saudi Arabia’s Faisal bin Farhan. Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia formed the Mecca defensive security pact in August, a grouping Egypt may join.
The European side was represented by Barrot, Miliband, Germany’s Johann Wadephul and Italy’s Antonio Tajani. The agenda covered the Palestinian issue, including settlement expansion, settler violence and the two-state solution, as well as security in the strait of Hormuz, Yemen and efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war and prevent spillover into the Black Sea.
Wadephul said: “We are united by the impact these deadlocked conflicts are having on the economy and security of our countries and by the will to seek new ways to bring about solutions.”
He made no criticism of the US but accused “the Houthis and Iran of blackmailing world trade and continuing to stranglehold global supplies of energy and fertiliser”.
“We are feeling the effects of the attacks on shipping routes and whether at the petrol pump or the supermarket,” he said. “Elsewhere there is threat of famine.”
Tajani said the aim of the meeting was to work for “de-escalation to guarantee freedom of navigation”.
“I do not believe the problem can be solved from a purely military standpoint,” he added. “If we want to reopen Hormuz, which is vital for our economies, we must promote dialogue and make Iran understand that this attitude cannot continue.”

STRASBOURG — The International Criminal Court has won this year's Sakharov Prize for Freedom of Thought, awarded by the European Parliament, according to two people with knowledge of the decision.
The €50,000 prize honors defenders of human rights and freedom of thought, with past winners including Nelson Mandela, Alexei Navalny, Belarusian journalists, and the people of Ukraine.

articles.title: Opening Ceremony of the 2026 Fair of Outstanding Vietnamese Export Products - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Opening Ceremony of the 2026 Fair of Outstanding Vietnamese Export Products  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
(Hochiminhcity.gov.vn) - On the afternoon of October 22nd, the HCMC Export 2026 Fair, showcasing typical Vietnamese export products, opened at the WTC Expo International Exhibition Center (Binh Duong Ward, Ho Chi Minh City).
The fair, organized by the Ministry of Industry and Trade in coordination with the People's Committee of Ho Chi Minh City, aims to promote trade connections, expand export markets, and enhance the competitiveness of Vietnamese businesses.
Attending the opening ceremony were Deputy Minister of Industry and Trade Phan Thi Thang; Standing Vice Chairman of the People's Committee of Ho Chi Minh City Nguyen Loc Ha; representatives from the Consulates General of several countries in Ho Chi Minh City; leaders of city departments and agencies, Departments of Industry and Trade of several southern provinces and cities; international buyers, and representatives of industry associations.
Ho Chi Minh City is stepping up trade connectivity.
In his opening remarks at the Fair, Standing Vice Chairman of the Ho Chi Minh City People's Committee Nguyen Loc Ha stated that in the first nine months of 2026, Ho Chi Minh City's Industrial Production Index (IIP) increased by 10.9%; total retail sales of goods and consumer service revenue reached over 1.4 trillion VND; and export turnover reached 76.01 billion USD, an increase of 10.6% compared to the same period.
These results further affirm Ho Chi Minh City's role as a major economic , financial, and commercial center and one of the leading growth engines of the country, in the context of a global economy still facing many difficulties and challenges.
Notably, the city's export structure is shifting towards increasing the proportion of high-quality, value-added processed and manufactured industrial products, agricultural products, and food items. This provides a foundation for businesses to enhance their competitiveness and adapt to the increasingly demanding requirements of the international market.
"In this context, Ho Chi Minh City is determined to continue accompanying and supporting businesses in expanding their markets, promoting green transformation, digital transformation , and participating more deeply in the global value chain," the Standing Vice Chairman of the City People's Committee emphasized.
City leaders expect the event to create strategic breakthroughs in promoting the "On-site Export" model; pioneering green transformation and digital transformation; and maximizing the O2O (Offline to Online) connectivity model.
Through this event, Ho Chi Minh City commits to always accompanying and creating a transparent and stable investment and business environment; promptly resolving difficulties and creating the most favorable conditions in terms of policies, logistics infrastructure and administrative procedures so that domestic and foreign businesses can confidently cooperate and develop in the long term.
You may also like
In her welcoming remarks, Deputy Minister of Industry and Trade Phan Thi Thang assessed that Ho Chi Minh City is a major economic center, a growth engine, and a trade and service hub of the Southern key economic region and the entire country. The city has always played a pioneering role in implementing the strategic directions of the Ministry of Industry and Trade.
Leaders of the Ministry of Industry and Trade highly appreciate the practical significance and strategic importance of the 2026 Vietnam Export Fair. This is not only a large-scale trade promotion event, but also a practical bridge between Vietnamese businesses and international buyers, contributing to boosting production, expanding markets, and enhancing the competitiveness of Vietnamese goods.
At the same time, we acknowledge and commend the proactive and decisive actions of the Ho Chi Minh City People's Committee; the active coordination of the Ho Chi Minh City Department of Industry and Trade, other departments, agencies, and industry associations in maintaining and enhancing the series of events that have practical significance for the industry and trade sector and the business community nationwide.
To ensure the Fair is effective and produces concrete results, the Deputy Minister of Industry and Trade expects the Vietnamese business community to continue proactively taking full advantage of the incentives from new-generation Free Trade Agreements (FTAs); constantly improving product quality, competitiveness, and standardizing production processes towards circular and green practices. On the part of state management agencies, the Ministry of Industry and Trade will continue to work alongside localities and businesses; perfecting the legal framework, promoting administrative reforms, supporting the removal of logistics difficulties, facilitating trade flows, and expanding international market opportunities.
Promoting green exports and developing sustainable supply chains.
The fair, held from October 22-24, 2026, brought together over 750 booths from businesses across the country and more than 400 buyers. Key product categories on display included food and agricultural products; textiles, leather goods and footwear; handicrafts, gifts, and wooden products; household appliances, metal products, hand tools; and export support services such as logistics, banking, insurance, and e-commerce.
One of the main focuses of the Fair is connecting Vietnamese businesses with international buyer networks from the United States, the European Union (EU), Japan, South Korea , China, and ASEAN; as well as connecting them with domestic distribution systems, supermarkets, e-commerce platforms, and wholesalers. B2B business networking activities, livestreaming product promotions, and factory and raw material area tours are organized to create more opportunities for cooperation and expand markets for Vietnamese products.
Within the framework of the Fair, on October 22nd, the Forum "Promoting Linkages Towards Green Exports" was held, with the theme "Flexible Supply Chains and Vietnam's Export Strategy in the Context of Diversification". On October 23rd, the International Conference "Green Production - Green Exports" was organized, focusing on the application of artificial intelligence (AI) and automation to improve productivity and increase export value.
In addition, the program includes workshops and training sessions to guide businesses in complying with new export standards such as CBAM, UKCA, Halal, and FDA; and support for e-commerce and direct exports through platforms like TikTok Shop and Amazon.
Through exhibitions, trade promotion activities, and direct networking, HCMC Export 2026 aims to support businesses in accessing domestic and international buyers and distribution systems; while promoting Vietnam's production capacity and strong products, contributing to promoting green exports and developing sustainable supply chains.
The fair also prioritizes products with registered quality standards, clear origin, and those that have been exported or have export potential; including products from businesses that have won the Ho Chi Minh City Golden Brand Award, businesses producing key products, potential products, and typical industrial and supporting industrial products of the city.

articles.title: Iran says 7 oil tankers attacked in the Strait of Hormuz as fears grow of a return to war - AP News
articles.summary: Iran says 7 oil tankers attacked in the Strait of Hormuz as fears grow of a return to war  AP NewsShip attacks in Strait of Hormuz hit record high in October  ReutersIran says seven ships hit in Hormuz Strait, warns US of wider response  Al JazeeraIran says 7 vessels hit near Strait of Hormuz, warns US of wider response  NewsNationStrait of Hormuz crisis traps 6,000 sailors as attacks on ships mount, UN maritime chief says  Fox News
articles.full_text:
TEL AVIV, Israel (AP) — Seven oil tankers caught fire or were damaged in the Strait of Hormuz overnight after being hit by Iran or striking naval mines, Tehran said Thursday, a markedly high number as tensions rise over concerns about a return to all-out war.
With days before a close election in Israel in which Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu could lose power, and before next month’s U.S. midterm election in which war-linked high prices have sparked voter anger, there are concerns that U.S.-Israeli attacks on Iran could resume.
“Netanyahu wants to attack Iran, that’s not even a question,” Danny Citrinowicz, a researcher at Israel’s Institute for National Security Studies and a former Iran specialist in Israel’s military and intelligence services, told The Associated Press.
He accused Israel of rushing into another round with Iran without revamping its strategy. A clear Netanyahu victory in the Oct. 27 election means an attack is almost guaranteed, he said.
Main opposition candidates are likely to focus on domestic issues first, but Citrinowicz said he believed the region is on the way toward “another kinetic escalation.”
Iran repeats threat to attack U.S. bases in the region
Iranian state television reported the claims about the latest attacks on ships, which the AP couldn’t independently confirm. The report cited the Revolutionary Guard Corps navy, which again threatened to strike U.S. military bases in the region if the U.S. keeps helping to guide commercial ships through the strait.
The report didn’t mention casualties. Iran still asserts control over the waterway, a central point of leverage in any talks with the U.S. over the war.
October has had the most reported attacks on commercial shipping since March in the war’s opening weeks, according to a British military monitor, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations. UKMTO didn’t report the latest attacks, but it has noted new reluctance by some shippers to report incidents.
Oil producers have found ways to keep crude flowing, experts say, but at a mounting cost.
Tankers continue moving through Strait of Hormuz despite attacks
Oil tankers are still moving oil through the strait under U.S. military protection despite the recent upsurge in attacks, according to shipping data and analysis company Lloyd’s List Intelligence.
Tanker operators willing to risk the voyage have been shuttling oil from Gulf producers through the strait at night with their location systems and mobile phones turned off using a U.S.-protected lane near the coast of Oman. Those tankers transfer oil to other tankers waiting in the Gulf of Oman for shipment to customers in Asia.
Those “active Gulf operators show little sign of retreating” despite 28 attacks on ships in October, the highest since the start of the war, Lloyd’s said in an online webinar Thursday.
The so-called “dark shuttle” overseen by U.S. Central Command has helped return oil shipments from the Gulf at roughly prewar levels, but at high costs in time, money and sailors’ lives. Spot charter rates for tankers have soared into the hundreds of thousands of dollars a day, while the ship-to-ship transfers can take several days.
UN urges US and Iran to return to diplomacy to end conflict, reopen strait
U.N. spokesman Stephane Dujarric said no commercial ships should be attacked and called for diplomacy between the U.S. and Iran to reopen the strait.
“For the sake of the people of the region and for the broader world, we need to see that waterway reopen, and we need to see tensions go down,” he told reporters Thursday.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on Wednesday said Tehran remains open to diplomacy, but is ready to defend itself.
Iran has warned that it learned important military lessons from the war that began with U.S. and Israeli attacks on Feb. 28, indicating in recent days that it could expand targets to include infrastructure such as undersea cables and data centers.
The United States, for its part, is sending more military assets to the region, including a third aircraft carrier and thousands of troops, to join the largest force of American warships and aircraft in the Middle East in decades.
Mediators, meanwhile, have been trying to bring Washington and Tehran back to formal talks.
Iran still promotes its latest proposal to end the war and fully open the strait within a week if the U.S. meets several conditions, including ending the U.S. blockade of Iranian ports. It echoes conditions in the deal that fell apart within days of both sides signing it in June.
U.S. President Donald Trump rejected the latest proposal last month, but both sides acknowledged that indirect discussions have continued.
The stakes are even higher if all-out war resumes
A return to full fighting would again endanger civilians throughout the region and complicate global deliveries of oil, natural gas and related products like fertilizer from the region and likely bring another spike in prices.
The head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, this week acknowledged that the Islamic Republic will suffer under a prolonged U.S. blockade. But economic pain and strategic collapse are not the same thing, he added, according to Iran’s state-run IRNA news agency.
Now the conflict has widened with the recent surge in fighting between Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia. The Saudi kingdom backs a coalition of forces with Yemen’s internationally recognized government that is fighting the rebels.
The Houthis’ repeated deadly attacks on airports and other facilities inside Saudi Arabia have pressured the close U.S. ally, which has sought military aid.
The escalation also has threatened a crucial shipping corridor, the Bab el-Mandeb at the southern end of the Red Sea.
Meanwhile, the president of Saudi oil company Aramco, whose sites have been targeted by the Houthis, said the amount of oil moving through a pipeline that bypasses the Strait of Hormuz has increased threefold in light of the global energy crisis.
The East-West pipeline’s capacity has surged from two million to seven million barrels each day, Amin Nasser said in an interview with Saudi-owned television Al Arabiya Business. He said the company has been using drones to assess any damage to the pipeline and help with firefighting.

U.S. intelligence finds Iran has "substantially increased" its efforts to target American diplomats and officials in the Middle East and beyond, with lethal plots reaching "advanced stages," according to an Oct. 23 memo to Secretary of State Marco Rubio obtained by Axios.
Why it matters: U.S. officials say the intelligence is one reason the State Department is drawing down personnel at several American embassies across the Middle East, amid mounting fears of a broader regional conflict.
U.S. officials also fear that Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen could expand their attacks beyond Saudi Arabia to other countries in the region.
Adding to the volatile security environment is the prospect of renewed U.S. and Israeli military operations against Iran, potentially after the midterm elections.
What they're saying: "We may do another little Operation Epic Fury, or [the Iranians] will agree [to a deal]," President Trump said at a rally in Florida on Friday.
"If they're smart, they will just say, 'Let's get down to business,' but I doubt they will do that because perhaps they're not smart."
Driving the news: In the one-page, unclassified memo obtained by Axios, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned Rubio that intelligence about Iranian assassination plots needs to reach more U.S. personnel than are currently authorized to receive it.
The memo does not identify specific targets, countries outside the Middle East or the nature of the plots, but says the underlying intelligence has already been shared with senior State Department officials.
Clayton offered to downgrade as much of the sensitive intelligence as possible so Rubio could share it more widely with personnel potentially at risk.
State of play: Earlier this week, the State Department ordered family members and nonessential personnel to leave the U.S. Embassy in Riyadh and consulates in Jeddah and Dhahran.
On Friday, the department also ordered reductions in U.S. diplomatic and government personnel at embassies in the United Arab Emirates, Lebanon, Qatar and Jordan, a U.S. official said.
"We decided that due to the threat of Houthi attacks and Iranian terror plots we need to reduce our footprint and keep only essential staff," the official said.
CNN first reported on the reduction in staffing at the four embassies.

articles.title: Shein Agrees to $100M US FTC Settlement Amid Regulatory Crackdown - Global Banking & Finance Review
articles.summary: Shein Agrees to $100M US FTC Settlement Amid Regulatory Crackdown  Global Banking & Finance Review
articles.full_text:
Shein Settles $100 Million FTC Probe as Regulatory Pressure Intensifies
By Helen Reid and Jody Godoy
Shein Faces Regulatory Scrutiny and Financial Penalties
FTC Investigation and Settlement Details
LONDON, Oct 23 (Reuters) - Chinese fast-fashion giant Shein has agreed to pay $100 million to settle an investigation by the US Federal Trade Commission over delivery delays and other customer complaints, a source with direct knowledge told Reuters on Friday.
The settlement, equivalent to 44% of Shein's second-quarter profit, is the latest to hit the online fast-fashion retailer facing a regulatory and tax crackdown in Europe and the US that has slammed the brakes on its growth.
Company Response and Ongoing Investigations
Shein, founded in China though headquartered in Singapore, said in a statement to Reuters that it had "reached a constructive outcome with the FTC", and that additional information would be shared soon. An FTC spokesperson declined to comment.
The company had warned in July filings for its Hong Kong IPO that the US probe could lead to significant fines.
Consumer Complaints and Delivery Issues
Consumers filed more than 12,000 complaints about Shein over more than $11 million in purchases between January 2020 and June 2026, according to FTC records reviewed by Reuters.
At least some of those relate to shipping, with customers reporting to the FTC and Better Business Bureau that they never received packages that Shein had marked as delivered, and that Shein customer service did not resolve the issue.
Reuters was not able to independently verify the substance of the complaints, or whether they were ultimately resolved.
Marketplace Operations and Third-Party Sellers
As well as selling its own-brand clothing, Shein's website also operates as a marketplace where third-party sellers offer everything from toys to household appliances and decor.
Impact of European Regulatory Changes
Increased Fees and Tariffs in the EU
MORE PAIN AHEAD FOR SHEIN WITH HIGHER EU FEES
Shein shares have already dropped 22% from their September 1 listing price as investors realised the extent to which the European Union's €3 fees on low-value e-commerce packages have bruised its business there.
And there's further pain ahead for Shein, with the EU imposing an additional €2 handling fee from November 1, making the total fee €5 per separate customs code.
Business Model Adjustments and Price Increases
"The way these tariffs are implemented is extra punishing for Shein," said Mike Ryan, head of e-commerce insights at Smarter Ecommerce, who has tracked how Shein has dialled down its spending on Google Ads visibility in Europe.
Shein was known for selling $5 dresses and $10 jeans, but has been forced to raise its prices as the US and then Europe closed customs duty loopholes.
CEO Sky Xu said last month that Shein would develop more higher-priced brands in an attempt to boost profitability.
Ongoing Legal and Regulatory Challenges
Shein is also still under investigation by the European Commission over illegal products on its marketplace. It was fined €150 million ($168 million) by France's data protection authority over the improper use of cookies last year.
FTC Actions Against Other Online Retailers
It's not the first time the US FTC has taken action against online retailers over deliveries.
US firm Fashion Nova was fined $9.3 million in 2020 for failing to meet shipping promises to customers and giving them gift cards instead of refunds.
Crocs Inc-owned Hey Dude was also fined $1.95 million in 2023 for failing to notify customers of shipping delays and suppressing negative reviews.
($1 = 0.8928 euros)
(Reporting by Helen Reid in London and Jody Godoy in New York; Editing by Adam Jourdan and Jan Harvey)

articles.title: Technological Development in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: Global Debates, Risks and Prospects for Albania - Tirana Times
articles.summary: Technological Development in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: Global Debates, Risks and Prospects for Albania  Tirana Times
articles.full_text:
By Denis Jukni
Artificial intelligence is rapidly moving from an experimental technology to a new infrastructure of the economy and public administration. Generative models, automation, robotics, cloud infrastructure, large-scale data processing and algorithmic systems are changing how companies produce, how institutions deliver services and how citizens receive information. This transformation opens opportunities to raise productivity, automate processes and improve public services. It also brings risks related to cybersecurity, privacy, algorithmic discrimination, disinformation, the labour market and the concentration of technological power.
For Albania, the question is no longer whether artificial intelligence will be used. It already is. The question is whether the country will manage to build the human, institutional, legal and technological capacities to use and control it.
From the race for algorithms to the race for infrastructure
The debate on artificial intelligence often focuses on models such as ChatGPT or Gemini. But the technological race is much broader. Developing AI requires considerable computing power, data centres, advanced processors, cloud services, large amounts of data, energy, capital and specialists.
The European Union makes this link explicit in its AI Continent Action Plan, built on computing infrastructure, data, skills, AI uptake and a trustworthy regulatory framework. In April 2026, the European Commission reported 19 “AI Factories” in Europe, with investment now extending to far larger “AI Gigafactories”.This adds a new dimension to the debate on digital sovereignty. A state can make extensive use of artificial intelligence while the models, processors, cloud infrastructure and platforms it relies on are controlled outside its territory.
For a small economy like Albania, replicating the entire global technology chain is not realistic. But it can build capacity to develop specialised applications, manage national data, audit algorithms, secure systems and avoid unnecessary dependence on a single technology supplier.
Innovation versus regulation
A central international debate concerns the line between innovation and control. Weak regulation can expose citizens and institutions to unsafe or discriminatory systems; poorly designed regulation can stifle innovation.
The European Union has opted for a risk-based approach through the Artificial Intelligence Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689. The Act entered into force in 2024, and significant parts of it already apply. Since 2 August 2026, the transparency obligations under Article 50, among other provisions, have been in effect. The logic is that not every use of AI carries the same risk: a system that recommends music cannot be treated like one that affects employment, education, public services or decisions with consequences for citizens.
Along the same lines, the OECD AI Principles call for transparency, explainability, safety, human oversight and accountability, including traceability throughout a system’s life cycle and the right of those adversely affected to understand and challenge an algorithmic outcome. UNESCO frames the issue directly in terms of human rights: dignity, privacy, fairness, transparency and human oversight must remain fundamental to the use of AI.
For Albania, these are no longer purely theoretical debates. In its Albania 2025 Report, the European Commission calls on the country to fully align with the AI Act and to put in place the structures needed to implement it.
Albania: rapid digitalisation, but a skills gap
Albania presents a striking contrast. According to the OECD’s Western Balkans Competitiveness Outlook 2024, the country has made considerable progress on digital society. Around 95% of public services were available online, and Albania ranked second in the Western Balkans on the digital society dimension.
Skills indicators, however, are far more problematic. Only 23.8% of individuals in Albania had basic or above-basic digital skills in OECD comparative data, compared with 34.8% in the Western Balkans and 53.9% in the EU. ICT specialists made up 2.6% of total employment, against 4.5% in the EU. Internet access, a digitalised administration and citizens’ ability to function in a digital environment are different things. Someone who uses a smartphone and social media every day is not necessarily able to recognise a sophisticated online scam, verify AI-generated material or understand an automated decision.
Albania compared with the Western Balkans and the EU
| Indicator | Albania | Western Balkans | EU | 
|---|---|---|---|
| OECD Digital Society index | 2.7 | 2.5 | n/a | 
| People with basic or above-basic digital skills | 23.8% | 34.8% | 53.9% | 
| ICT specialists in employment | 2.6% | 2.8% | 4.5% | 
| Public services available online | approx. 95% | n/a | n/a | 
| Enterprises using AI | 12.4% (2026) | n/a | 20.0% (2025) | 
The table highlights a central contradiction: public administration has digitalised faster than the population has acquired digital skills. This human capital gap may limit Albania’s ability not only to use the technology, but also to develop, audit and control it.
Albanian businesses are entering the AI era
According to INSTAT data published on 21 September 2026, 12.4% of Albanian enterprises with 10 or more employees use artificial intelligence technologies, up from 9% a year earlier. Among large enterprises, the figure reaches 28.1%. Meanwhile, 35.3% of enterprises use cloud services and 34.5% employ ICT specialists. Uptake is growing quickly but remains below the EU level: according to Eurostat, around 20% of EU enterprises with at least 10 employees used AI in 2025.
The long-term problem runs deeper. The OECD finds that Albania performs above the Western Balkans average in most competitiveness dimensions, but below it in science, technology and innovation. Low investment in research and development, weak links between universities and business, and relatively modest scientific output limit the country’s capacity to move from being a user of technology to a creator of it.
Diella: from virtual assistant to public decision-making
Albania is also experimenting with AI in a far more sensitive field: state administration.
Diella was launched in January 2025 as the virtual assistant of the e-Albania portal. According to government figures, she had recorded 972,000 interactions by September of that year. She was then given the role of Minister of State for Artificial Intelligence, under the authority of the Prime Minister.
What matters is not the avatar or the title, but the functions to be delegated to the technology.
In 2026, the government announced that it is building an AI-supported electronic procurement system. According to the official description, it is meant to cover everything from market research and bid submission to contract monitoring. The government also states that Diella will be able to draw data from more than 40 public registers and that the process will be traceable and subject to manual review. These are the government’s objectives and claims about a system still under construction, not evidence that the problems of public procurement have been solved.
This is precisely where the question of algorithmic accountability arises. If an AI system influences a procurement procedure, who is responsible when it makes a mistake? Can it be established which data shaped the outcome? What happens if a state register contains inaccurate data? Can an economic operator obtain an explanation and challenge the result? Who has access to the system logs? Who audits the algorithms and the changes made to them?
These questions carry even more weight given the economic importance of public procurement and the European Commission’s repeated calls to strengthen competition, administrative capacity and professionalisation in the sector.
The use of AI in procurement may bring more automation and traceability, but technology does not by itself eliminate conflicts of interest, manipulation or corruption. If processes, data or control mechanisms are flawed, automation can reproduce those flaws on a larger scale.
Employment: transformation rather than sudden job losses
A major fear is that machines will replace workers.
A 2025 study by the International Labour Organization (ILO) estimates that one in four workers worldwide is in an occupation with some degree of exposure to generative AI. Only 3.3% of global employment falls into the highest exposure category. The ILO’s key conclusion is that, because most occupations still require human input, jobs are more likely to be transformed than eliminated outright.
In Albania, this could affect administration, finance, accounting, call centres, translation, media, legal services and other professions built largely on processing text and information. The challenge is not only how many jobs might be lost, but whether Albanian workers will acquire the skills to use AI as a productivity tool.
Risks: from cyberattacks to a crisis of trust
Artificial intelligence does not create one new category of risk so much as amplify existing ones. In cybersecurity, AI can help detect anomalies and attacks, but it can also be used to automate phishing and social engineering, produce convincing fraudulent content and analyse targets.
For Albania, this matters particularly after the major cyberattacks on government systems in 2022 and 2023. The OECD notes progress in aligning the cybersecurity framework with the EU acquis, but also challenges in ensuring the resilience of critical information infrastructure. Law No. 25/2024 “On Cybersecurity” and the National Cybersecurity Strategy 2025-2030 aim at alignment with European standards, including the NIS2 Directive.
Yet there is a paradox: the more state services, registers and algorithms are interconnected, the greater both the benefits of data exchange and the damage if they are compromised.

articles.title: Pharmaceutical Supply Chains and Drug Shortages - Kings Research
articles.summary: Pharmaceutical Supply Chains and Drug Shortages  Kings Research
articles.full_text:
The healthcare sector relies entirely upon consistent medicine availability to function properly. Based on Kings Research analysis, the global pharmaceuticals market size reached USD 1,620.12 billion in 2025. Projections anticipate it hitting USD 2,763.69 billion by 2033, advancing at a 7.02% compound annual growth rate from 2026 to 2033. This massive expansion demands highly reliable infrastructure to support global populations. Pharmaceutical drug shortages occur when available supply fails to meet current or projected demand. Common causes include manufacturing quality problems, production delays, shortages of active pharmaceutical ingredients, regulatory delays, unexpected increases in demand, and product discontinuations. Limited production capacity and dependence on a small array of suppliers make disruptions harder to resolve. To support this growth uninterrupted, pharmaceutical companies seek new methods to secure their operations.
Pharmaceutical companies face intense pressure to deliver critical therapies to patients across the globe. The global supply network spans multiple continents, involving countless facilities, logistics providers, and regulatory bodies. Every step in this complex web must function flawlessly. When one link breaks, the entire system suffers, leading to delayed treatments and severe health complications for patients waiting for life-saving medications. Supply chain professionals within pharmaceutical companies work tirelessly to identify vulnerabilities before they cause systemic failures. They rely on detailed data, advanced analytics, and strategic partnerships to maintain a steady flow of materials. The ultimate goal is to ensure that every patient receives their prescribed medication exactly when they require it, avoiding delays or compromises in quality. Achieving this goal requires massive coordination, immense capital investment, and a deep understanding of global trade dynamics.
Why Are Pharmaceutical Supply Chains Becoming More Vulnerable to Drug Shortages?
Vulnerabilities arise when the supply chain lacks diversification and flexibility. A nationwide drug shortage differs completely from a localized distribution delay. When a national shortage happens, the total output across all manufacturers fails to cover patient needs across the entire country. This systemic failure forces hospitals and pharmacies to ration life-saving treatments, directly impacting patient health outcomes.
According to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) Annual Report on Drug Shortages for Calendar Year 2023, the agency tracked 55 new shortages during the year, highlighting the severe pressure on production networks. At the same time, the FDA actively worked to prevent 236 additional shortages through early intervention and regulatory flexibility. Despite these efforts, the total count of active ongoing shortages stood at 98 by the end of 2023. These figures demonstrate the immense challenge pharmaceutical companies face in maintaining consistent supply levels across thousands of essential products.
The issue matters significantly for everyone involved in healthcare delivery. Hospitals struggle to source essential medicines, forcing doctors to alter treatment plans, use less effective alternatives, or delay critical surgeries. Pharmacies spend countless hours attempting to locate alternative medications for their patients, increasing administrative burdens and driving up operational costs. Patients bear the ultimate burden, experiencing heightened anxiety, prolonged illness, and potential adverse health effects when their prescribed therapies become unavailable. Manufacturers must address underlying vulnerabilities, such as relying heavily on a single facility or supplier. By doing so, they can build a resilient system capable of withstanding unexpected disruptions and ensuring consistent medicine availability for all patients.
How Does a Pharmaceutical Supply Chain Move From Raw Materials to Finished Medicines?
The product journey involves multiple highly regulated stages, requiring precise coordination between various specialized entities. Active pharmaceutical ingredients (API) and excipients serve as the foundational building blocks for all medications. Chemical manufacturers carefully synthesize these raw materials in highly controlled environments. Following synthesis, the API undergoes rigorous testing to ensure absolute purity and compliance with strict quality standards set by health authorities.
Once the API passes all required tests, it moves to the finished dose formulation stage. Here, pharmaceutical companies blend the active ingredients with excipients to create the final pill, capsule, or liquid medication. This stage demands extreme precision to guarantee accurate dosing, proper absorption rates, and consistent therapeutic effects. After formulation, the product proceeds to the quality release phase. Independent quality assurance teams meticulously review batch records and conduct final analytical tests before approving the medication for distribution.
The approved products are then packaged securely to prevent contamination or degradation during transit. Logistics providers transport the packaged medicines in climate controlled vehicles to regional warehouses, wholesalers, and ultimately to pharmacies and hospitals.
To improve visibility across this complex journey, major pharmaceutical companies are investing heavily in advanced tracking systems. In June 2023, Sanofi announced the rollout of plai, an artificial intelligence application developed in partnership with Aily Labs, across its supply chain operations. Implementation within its biopharma supply chain enabled Sanofi to predict 80% of low inventory positions. This advancement allows supply chain teams to take early mitigating actions to secure supply faster than ever before. Digital tools provide immediate alerts regarding potential bottlenecks, enabling rapid corrective actions to maintain a steady supply flow. Supply chain managers utilize these systems to trace every batch of medication back to its original raw materials, ensuring complete accountability at every step.
Pharmaceutical Supply Chain Stages
| Supply Stage | Main Vulnerability | Early Warning Indicator | Mitigation | 
| Raw Materials | Sourcing concentration | Supplier lead time increases | Alternative supplier qualification | 
| API Production | Quality failures | Failed batches during testing | Enhanced quality control systems | 
| Finished Dose | Equipment breakdown | Maintenance alerts | Capacity redundancy | 
| Distribution | Logistics delays | Transport bottleneck alerts | Regional warehousing | 
By understanding these stages and their associated vulnerabilities, pharmaceutical companies can implement targeted strategies to strengthen the entire network and prevent future disruptions. Each stage represents a critical link that requires constant monitoring, rigorous auditing, and proactive management.
Why Does Dependence on a Limited Pool of API Suppliers Create Supply Risks?
Geographic concentration of API production creates severe upstream dependencies that threaten the stability of the entire healthcare system. Many pharmaceutical companies rely heavily on single source procurement for key starting materials and chemical intermediates. When a single facility experiences a delay, the entire downstream system stalls, leading to rapid inventory depletion. Transport restrictions, severe weather events, and geopolitical tensions further complicate supplier substitution, making it incredibly difficult to pivot quickly during a crisis.
A June 2021 White House supply chain review highlighted the U.S. pharmaceutical industry's reliance on overseas manufacturing, finding that approximately 87% of FDA-registered facilities producing active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) for generic drugs were located outside the United States as of March 2021. Separately, the U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO) reported that 73% of FDA-registered API manufacturing facilities serving the U.S. market were located overseas during the same period. This massive geographic concentration means a localized disruption abroad ripples globally, impacting medicine availability worldwide. If a major API manufacturing plant experiences a prolonged shutdown, pharmaceutical companies across multiple continents will simultaneously struggle to secure the necessary materials to continue production.
To mitigate this extreme reliance, industry leaders are taking decisive action to expand their domestic manufacturing capabilities. By bringing API production closer to home, pharmaceutical companies reduce their exposure to international shipping delays, port congestions, and global supply chain bottlenecks. Regionalizing the supply base creates a strong buffer against international trade disputes and unexpected export restrictions imposed by foreign governments.
Building new API facilities requires massive capital investments and years of regulatory approvals. Therefore, pharmaceutical companies must carefully balance the benefits of domestic production with the associated costs. They must prioritize the most critical APIs and develop long term strategies to ensure a steady supply of these essential materials. Reducing dependence on a limited pool of suppliers remains a critical step toward achieving true supply chain resilience and protecting patient health globally.
Which Manufacturing and Market Conditions Trigger Pharmaceutical Drug Shortages?
Manufacturing quality failures and the resulting corrective actions frequently trigger massive supply disruptions. When a facility fails a regulatory inspection or discovers impurities in a batch, production must halt immediately. The time required to investigate the root cause, implement corrective measures, and revalidate the equipment can lead to months of reduced output. articles.title: Austrians spent 16% of retail expenditure online - Ecommerce News - Europe
articles.summary: Austrians spent 16% of retail expenditure online  Ecommerce News - Europe
articles.full_text:
In 2025, more than 16 percent of Austrian consumer spending in retail was generated online. A year earlier, the online share of consumer retail spending came to 14.9 percent. This brings the market volume of ecommerce in the country in 2025 to approximately 12.4 billion euros.
This is according to an analysis by RegioData Research on Austrian online consumer spending. In 2025, Austrians spent around 1,400 euros per person annually on online purchases. When looking at different retail sectors, it becomes evident that some have a bigger online share than others.
Shares by sector
The consumer electronics sector has an online share of 43 percent of consumer spending. It is followed by footwear, with an online share of around 36 percent. Personal goods also have a large online share (33 percent), and so do clothing and books (each around 31 percent).
Consumer spending in other European countries
The report also looked at online consumer spending in other European countries. It seems that Austria is somewhere in the middle. The United Kingdom leads the ranking in Europe, with an online share of 29.3 percent. Austria’s online share is almost as high as the share in Germany (16.8 percent). Serbia, on the other hand, has one of the lowest shares with 6.7 percent.
Cross-border stores have majority market share
In Austria, just over 40 percent of online spending goes to local online stores. The majority goes to cross-border sellers. When looking at the top online sellers in the country, it becomes evident that Amazon has the biggest market share (35.1 percent). It is followed by Temu (5.1 percent) and eBay (4.1 percent). Chinese online sellers (Temu, Shein and AliExpress) have a combined market share of 7.9 percent.

articles.title: Dubai Humanitarian drives global supply chain resilience at AidEx - STAT Times
articles.summary: Dubai Humanitarian drives global supply chain resilience at AidEx  STAT Times
articles.full_text:
At AidEx 2026 in Geneva, Dubai Humanitarian emphasised the urgent need for a stronger Global Safety Net and resilient supply chains amid growing crises.
As the world faces an unprecedented number of complex crises, the need for a robust and adaptive approach to delivering life-saving aid has never been more critical. Recognising this global imperative, Dubai Humanitarian took centre stage at AidEx 2026, held on the 21st and 22nd of October in Geneva, Switzerland. Throughout the prestigious two-day exhibition, the organisation showcased its unique humanitarian ecosystem, driving forward vital conversations on how to build supply chains that are not only more resilient and connected but also highly diversified.
During the event, Dubai Humanitarian actively engaged with a wide spectrum of humanitarian organisations, international partners, and private-sector commercial companies. The organisation utilised its exhibition stand as a dynamic platform to introduce the myriad of opportunities offered by its free zone, underscoring its pivotal role in supporting global humanitarian action. It highlighted the vast capabilities of its international community, extended an open invitation to potential new members, and detailed its ongoing efforts to establish a comprehensive Global Safety Net. This ambitious initiative aims to seamlessly connect humanitarian hubs, critical resources, operational data, and logistical capabilities across different regions of the world.
A major highlight of their participation was the convening of a high-level session titled “Sustaining Humanitarian Response Under Pressure: Partners in Motion for a Stronger Global Safety Net.” This panel brought together some of the most influential humanitarian organisations and global logistics providers to closely examine how international cooperation can be optimised to sustain the delivery of critical assistance amidst escalating global disruptions.
In his welcoming remarks, Giuseppe Saba, CEO of Dubai Humanitarian, highlighted the importance of sustained international dialogue and cooperation in strengthening humanitarian preparedness: “Over the past years, we have consistently brought together humanitarian organisations with government and logistics partners to address the challenges facing global humanitarian supply chains. Through these ongoing exchanges, we have built a shared understanding that resilience requires more than responding to disruptions. It requires preparedness, diversified routes, connected systems and partnerships that can be mobilised when they are needed most. Our focus today is to continue translating this collective understanding into stronger coordination and practical solutions that keep humanitarian assistance moving, even under the most challenging circumstances,” said Saba.
The panel, expertly moderated by Benjamin Safari, Head of Supply Management Service at UNHCR, featured a diverse array of industry leaders. Participants included Alex Marianelli, Chief Inter Agency Supply Chain Services at the World Food Programme; Cecile Terraz, Global Director, Humanitarian Services & Supply Chain Management at the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies; Grete Kjaer, Global Key Client Manager, Aid & Relief at A.P. Moller-Maersk; Jean-Cédric Meeùs, Chief Global Transport & Logistics at UNICEF; and Sayed Harris, Manager of Cargo Global Commercial & Special Products at Emirates SkyCargo.
The profound discussion addressed the increasing pressure placed on humanitarian operations due to active conflicts, maritime insecurity, airspace restrictions, and severe disruptions to traditional transport corridors. These logistical hurdles are further complicated by the harsh reality of growing humanitarian needs combined with constrained operational funding. The leaders explored how humanitarian entities and private-sector logistics providers can forge closer alliances to anticipate future disruptions, diversify their transport routes, and improve the real-time visibility of humanitarian supplies. They also discussed strengthening coordination across procurement, compliance, and emergency logistics, emphasising the strategic role of humanitarian hubs in supporting global preparedness and exploring opportunities for greater interoperability and shared infrastructure.
Established in 2003 under the visionary leadership of His Highness Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, Vice President and Prime Minister of the UAE and Ruler of Dubai, Dubai Humanitarian stands today as an independent free-zone authority and the world’s largest humanitarian hub. Hosting over 80 members, including United Nations agencies, non-profit organisations, and commercial enterprises, the hub maintains an impressive average of $200 million in prepositioned humanitarian supplies, ensuring a rapid and effective international emergency response when the world needs it most.

articles.title: Revised Forecasts, RBA Letter Confirm Treasurer's Inflation Agenda - Mirage News
articles.summary: Revised Forecasts, RBA Letter Confirm Treasurer's Inflation Agenda  Mirage News
articles.full_text:
"Taxaholic Treasurer Jim Chalmers has finally admitted his economic agenda is delivering slower growth and higher unemployment, but rather than undo the damage from his active inflation agenda he continues to stoke inflation through deficits and public spending pushing up interest rates and prices at the supermarket", said Shadow Treasurer, Tim Wilson.
Mr Wilson's comments come in the wake of the Treasurer flagging growth and unemployment downgrades ahead of MYEFO, and the Reserve Bank confirming in writing to a parliamentary committee that lower government spending would reduce inflationary pressures.
"Small businesses and families are living the consequences of our Taxaholic Treasurer's active inflation agenda every day with higher taxes, 16 interest rate rises and higher prices at the supermarket".
"The Reserve Bank has now put in writing what every household already knows. When the government spends less, inflation comes down and the pressure comes off interest rates".
"Real government spending grew by 4.3 per cent last financial year, more than double what was forecast, yet the Treasurer still wants Australians to believe inflation is everyone's fault but his".
"Underlying inflation lifted above the RBA's target in July 2025, and it still isn't under control which means higher mortgage rates and supermarket prices and all because the Treasurer can't kick his spending addiction".
"A sugar hit of data centre investment isn't going to solve our Taxaholic Treasurer running down small businesses, households and confidence".
"The Reserve Bank and the International Monetary Fund have warned government spending is fuelling inflation so it might be time for the Treasurer to start listening".
"Markets are now betting on another rate rise in November, and economists are putting a 50-50 chance on recession. Our Titanic Treasurer has been warned about the iceberg of taxes, spending and regulation, and his only response is to shout, "full steam ahead"".
"The Coalition has a plan to turn this around. We will put a speed limit on spending so government can't spend faster than the economy is growing, crack down on the waste, fraud and abuse of public money that is stoking inflation, and deliver our Tax Back Guarantee so every Australian worker gets a bigger, permanent tax cut, every year".
"Lower taxes and lower inflation give small businesses the confidence to invest, hire and grow, and give families the breathing room to get ahead again".
"The Treasurer has a choice in MYEFO. He can rein in spending, or he can keep running the economy down the recession runway and leave households and small businesses to pay for a recession Australia doesn't have to have".

Economist Tyler Cowen joins David Wolpe for a conversation about AI, religion, and what makes us human. Tyler makes the case that AI’s biggest impact may be on status: who gains it, who loses it, and what happens to experts like rabbis when anyone can ask ChatGPT all their questions. articles.full_text: The OCC, as part of its continuing effort to reduce paperwork and respondent burden, invites comment on a new information collection, as required by the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (PRA). In accordance with the requirements of the PRA, the OCC may not conduct or sponsor, and the respondent is not required to respond to an information collection unless it displays a currently valid Office of Management and Budget (OMB) control number. The OCC is proposing a new information collection titled "Reporting Forms and Instructions for Permitted Payment Stablecoin Issuers Subject to the Jurisdiction of the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency," that would include weekly and quarterly reporting forms that must be completed by permitted payment stablecoin issuers and foreign payment stablecoin issuers. The OCC is seeking a new OMB control number for this information collection. The OCC also is giving notice that it has sent the collection to OMB for review.

SUMMARY:
The Department of State has submitted the information collections described below to the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for approval. We are soliciting public comments to permit the Department to:
Evaluate whether the proposed information collection is necessary for the proper functions of the Department.
Evaluate the accuracy of our estimate of the time and cost burden for this proposed collection, including the validity of the methodology and assumptions used.
Enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to be collected.
Minimize the reporting burden on those who are to respond, including the use of automated collection techniques or other forms of information technology.
Please note that comments submitted in response to this Notice are public record. Before including any detailed personal information, you should be aware that your comments as submitted, including your personal information, will be available for public review.
Abstract of Proposed Collection
1405-0011, DS-2029,Application for Consular Report of Birth Abroad of a Citizen of the United States of America:
The form is used to apply for a Consular Report of Birth Abroad of a U.S. citizen. The information collected on this form will be used to certify the acquisition of U.S. citizenship at birth of a person born abroad. 8 U.S.C. 1104 and 22 CFR 50.5-50.7 are among the important legal authorities pertaining to the Department's use of this form.
1405-0187, DS-5507,Affidavit of Physical Presence or Residence, Parentage, and Support:
The form is used to determine whether a U.S. national parent has met the statutory physical presence or residence requirements to transmit U.S. nationality to his/her child born abroad or in a United States territory for U.S. noncitizen nationality; to establish parentage of the child; and to fulfill the requirements of 8 U.S.C. 1409(a), which permits acknowledgment of paternity under oath and requires the U.S. citizen father's written agreement to provide financial support for a child born abroad out of wedlock to a U.S. citizen father.
Methodology
Parents normally apply for a Consular Report of Birth Abroad at a U.S. embassy or consulate in the consular district in which the birth occurred. A consular officer will interview the parent(s)/guardian, examine the application and supporting documentation, and enter the information provided into the Department of State American Citizen Services (ACS) electronic database. The DS-2029 application is also available in an online format known as eCRBA. eCRBA allows applicants to enter their data, upload required documents, pay fees, and schedule an appointment to appear at the adjudicating post for an interview. Additionally, the applicant may check the status of their application.
Parent(s) may complete and submit the Affidavit of Physical Presence or Residence, Parentage, and Support in person or by mail. The form may be accessed online, completed electronically, printed, and signed; or it may be downloaded, printed, and completed manually.
Paul T. Peek,
Acting Managing Director for Passport Support Operations, Bureau of Consular Affairs, Passport Services, Department of State.

articles.title: Fisheries of the Exclusive Economic Zone Off Alaska; Pacific Cod by Catcher Vessels Using Trawl Gear in the Central Regulatory Area of the Gulf of Alaska
articles.summary: NMFS is prohibiting directed fishing for Pacific cod by catcher vessels using trawl gear in the Central Regulatory Area of the Gulf of Alaska (GOA). This action is necessary to prevent exceeding the 2026 total allowable catch (TAC) of Pacific cod allocated to catcher vessels using trawl gear in the Central Regulatory Area of the GOA.
articles.full_text:
AGENCY:
National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Commerce.
                    ACTION:
Temporary rule; closure.
                    SUMMARY:
NMFS is prohibiting directed fishing for Pacific cod by catcher vessels using trawl gear in the Central Regulatory Area of the Gulf of Alaska (GOA). This action is necessary to prevent exceeding the 2026 total allowable catch (TAC) of Pacific cod allocated to catcher vessels using trawl gear in the Central Regulatory Area of the GOA.
                    DATES:
Effective 1200 hours, Alaska local time (A.l.t.), October 21, 2026, through 2400 hours, A.l.t., December 31, 2026.
            
                SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
NMFS manages the groundfish fishery in the GOA exclusive economic zone according to the Fishery Management Plan for Groundfish of the GOA (FMP) prepared and recommended by the North Pacific Fishery Management Council under authority of the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act (Magnuson-Stevens Act). Regulations governing fishing by U.S. vessels in accordance with the FMP appear at subpart H of 50 CFR part 600 and 50 CFR part 679.
The annual 2026 Pacific cod TAC allocated to catcher vessels using trawl gear in the Central Regulatory Area of the GOA not participating in the cooperative fishery of the Rockfish Program is 7,782 metric tons (mt) as established by the final 2026 and 2027 harvest specifications for groundfish in the GOA (91 FR 11902, March 11, 2026).
The Regional Administrator, Alaska Region, NMFS (Regional Administrator) has determined that the annual 2026 Pacific cod TAC allocated to catcher vessels using trawl gear in the Central Regulatory Area of the GOA will be, or has been, reached. Therefore, in accordance with § 679.20(d)(1)(i) and (d)(1)(ii)(B), the Regional Administrator is establishing a directed fishing allowance of 5,782 mt and is setting aside the remaining 2,000 mt as incidental catch to support other anticipated groundfish fisheries. The Regional Administrator finds that this directed fishing allowance will be or has been reached. Consequently, in accordance with § 679.20(d)(1)(iii), NMFS is prohibiting directed fishing for Pacific cod caught by catcher vessels using trawl gear in the Central Regulatory Area of the GOA to prevent exceeding this sector's annual allocation of Pacific cod TAC.
While this closure is effective the maximum retainable amounts at § 679.20(e) and (f) apply at any time during a trip. This closure does not apply to fishing by vessels participating in the cooperative fishery of the Rockfish Program in the Central Regulatory Area of the GOA.
Classification
NMFS issues this action pursuant to section 305(d) of the Magnuson-Stevens Act. This action is required by 50 CFR part 679, which was issued pursuant to section 304(b) of the Magnuson-Stevens Act, and is exempt from review under Executive Order 12866.
Pursuant to 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B), there is good cause to waive prior notice and an opportunity for public comment on this action, as notice and comment would be impracticable and contrary to the public interest, as it would prevent NMFS from responding to the most recent fisheries data on the catch of Pacific cod in a timely fashion and would delay the closure of Pacific cod by catcher vessels using trawl gear in the Central Regulatory Area of the GOA. NMFS was unable to publish a notice providing time for public comment because the most recent, relevant data regarding catch of Pacific cod by catcher vessels using trawl gear in the Central Regulatory Area of the GOA only became available as of October 20, 2026.
There is good cause under 5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3) to establish an effective date less than 30 days after date of publication. This finding is based upon the reasons provided above for waiver of prior notice and opportunity for public comment.
                    
                    
                        16 U.S.C. 1801 
                        et seq.
                
                    Dated: October 20, 2026. 
Shannon Bettridge, 
Acting Director, Office of Sustainable Fisheries, National Marine Fisheries Service.

This document has been published in the Federal Register. Use the PDF linked in the document sidebar for the official electronic format.
AGENCY:
National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Commerce.
ACTION:
Temporary rule; closure.
SUMMARY:
NMFS is prohibiting directed fishing for pollock in Statistical Area 620 in the Gulf of Alaska (GOA). This action is necessary to prevent exceeding the annual 2026 total allowable catch (TAC) of pollock in Statistical Area 620 in the GOA.
DATES:
Effective 1200 hours, Alaska local time (A.l.t.), October 21, 2026 through 2400 hours, A.l.t., December 31, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Abby Jahn, 907-586-7228.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
NMFS manages the groundfish fishery in the GOA exclusive economic zone according to the Fishery Management Plan for Groundfish of the Gulf of Alaska (FMP) prepared and recommended by the North Pacific Fishery Management Council under
( printed page 66793)
authority of the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act (Magnuson-Stevens Act). Regulations governing fishing by U.S. vessels in accordance with the FMP appear at subpart H of 50 CFR part 600 and 50 CFR part 679.
The annual 2026 TAC of pollock in Statistical Area 620 in the GOA is 60,477 metric tons (mt) as established by the final 2026 and 2027 harvest specifications for groundfish in the GOA (91 FR 11902, March 11, 2026).
The Regional Administrator, Alaska Region, NMFS (Regional Administrator) has determined that the annual 2026 TAC of pollock in Statistical Area 620 in the GOA will be or has been reached. Therefore, in accordance with § 679.20(d)(1)(i) and 679.20(d)(1)(ii)(B), the Regional Administrator is establishing a directed fishing allowance of 60,277 mt and is setting aside the remaining 200 mt as incidental catch because it is necessary to support other anticipated groundfish fisheries. The Regional Administrator finds that this directed fishing allowance will be or has been reached. Consequently, in accordance with § 679.20(d)(1)(iii), NMFS is prohibiting directed fishing for pollock in Statistical Area 620 in the GOA to prevent exceeding the annual apportionment of pollock TAC for this area.
While this closure is effective, the maximum retainable amounts at § 679.20(e) and (f) apply at any time during a trip.
Classification
NMFS issues this action pursuant to section 305(d) of the Magnuson-Stevens Act. This action is required by 50 CFR part 679, which was issued pursuant to section 304(b) of the Magnuson-Stevens Act, and is exempt from review under Executive Order 12866.
Pursuant to 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B), there is good cause to waive prior notice and an opportunity for public comment on this action, as notice and comment would be impracticable and contrary to the public interest, as it would prevent NMFS from responding to the most recent fisheries data on pollock catch in a timely fashion, and would delay the closure of directed fishing for pollock in Statistical Area 620 in the GOA. NMFS was unable to publish a notice providing time for public comment because the most recent, relevant data on pollock catch in Statistical Area 620 in the GOA only became available as of October 21, 2026.
There is good cause under 5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3) to establish an effective date less than 30 days after date of publication. This finding is based upon the reasons provided above for waiver of prior notice and opportunity for public comment.
